newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus tensions may hit business, tourism.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus tensions may hit business, tourism.

text.p: The Cyprus government's decision to buy missiles from Russia could harm the eastern Mediterranean island's lucrative tourist trade and its overall economy if tension persists, tourism and investment sources said on Wednesday.

Tension on the island has been ratcheted upwards by disclosure of government plans to buy the anti-aircraft missiles and by the threats from Turkey of a pre-emptive strike if the missiles are delivered.

"It is a bit early to say how this will affect business because decisions are being made at the moment. My feeling is if it goes out of the news the impact will be minimal," said Noel Josephides, chairman of the Association of Greek Cypriot Travel Agents.

"If it continues day and night...what will begin to happen is that people will say, 'If there is a risk of going to Cyprus I have a very wide choice in the world, why should I go to a place where my holiday is likely to be disrupted?'."

The island relies heavily on tourism, which provides 21 percent of gross domestic product. About two million tourists visit the southern areas of the island each year, spending around 800 million pounds ($1.7 billion), representing 40 percent of total foreign currency earnings.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkish forces occupied the northern third of the island in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup which was engineered by the military then in power in Greece.
Last year four Greek Cypriots and one Turkish Cypriot were killed in incidents along the ceasefire line which snakes across the island, in the worst violence since 1974.

Josephides, who is based in Britain and specialises in Cyprus tours, said the most optimistic estimate this year would be a five percent increase in British tourists to Cyprus, compared with the 12 percent drop in 1996.
The Cyprus Tourism Organisation says it has no feedback that the political situation could have an effect. "We have had no reaction from our markets," said CTO spokesman Kyriakos Iacovides.
But he said that 1997 was expected to be a difficult year in any case because of tougher competition from new destinations in Southeast Asia and the Caribbean.
Stavros Agrotis of the Cyprus Investment and Securities Corporation (CISCO) attributed a 2.14 percent drop in shares on the Cyprus Stock Exchange (CSE) between January 3 and 14 to the tension.
He said that if the market were a little more sensitive to political developments the drop would have been higher.
"My feeling is that somehow people in Cyprus are becoming a bit immune to the political situation - that explains why there wasn't a more significant drop in shares." he said.
"The market feels that shares are close to their lowest point," he explained. "Over the past few days we have been net sellers because of the political uncertainty."
The tension is also affecting overall business activity. "I get feedback from the banks and there is a reduction in the enquiries for loans," said Agrotis.
A senior economist at a leading local bank agreed that demand had declined, but said it had nothing to do with the recent tensions.

"People are still trying to understand what it all means... if the tension, which I think is receding, were to continue for another one or two months people would say to themselves 'Things are not good so I won't spend my money,'" the economist said.
But he agreed that an escalation of tension could have devastating effects on the economy.

"Just a flight of Turkish airforce planes low over Ayia Napa would cause havoc," he said, referring to the southeastern tourist resort where thousands of tourists flock every year. "It doesn't take much to destroy what one has built."
($=0.47 pounds)
